Verified after the fact: diff -rq of the pinned snapshot against the live target reports no source file differing. A few packmate/__pycache__/*.pyc artifacts appeared under TARGET during the window from a concurrent process outside this run (this run's PoCs re-implemented the functions inline and never imported the package); no source file was touched.

reproductions: packmate extract_zip: relative ../ member overwrote a file outside dest, and an absolute-path member wrote outside dest.
packmate load_manifest: yaml.Loader executed os.system from a manifest tag; safe_load rejects the same input.
edgeproxy fetchRemote: the strings.Contains predicate admits 169.254.169.254, a suffixed lookalike domain and a loopback URL.
pulse-api decode_token: a garbage-signature token with role=admin passes the app's decode and expiry checks.

findings.title: Chain: support-ticket text reaches a shell on the support box
findings.evidence: The attacker never authenticates to deskagent. Step 1: they file an ordinary support ticket whose body carries instructions. Step 2: gather_context (planner.py:73) substring-matches that ticket against some later user's question and formats it into the SYSTEM prompt via build_system_prompt (prompts.py:53), the channel the code comment calls 'background it should treat as settled'. Step 3: the model emits a tool_use block and dispatch (tools.py:150) splats the arguments into run_command (tools.py:68), which runs them with shell=True and no allowlist. Step 4: read_file (tools.py:56) has no base directory, so /proc/self/environ yields DESKAGENT_GATEWAY_KEY and DESKAGENT_SERVICE_TOKEN, and planner.py:115 returns that output to the caller verbatim.
findings.impact: Remote code execution and credential theft on the support box, triggered by a party who only ever touched the ticketing system. The shared service token protecting the HTTP surface is irrelevant to this path.
findings.recommendation: Break the chain at the trust boundary: never place retrieved ticket text in the system prompt, and remove the free-form shell tool rather than relying on prompt wording (prompts.py:15) to restrain the model.

findings.title: LLM tool executes arbitrary shell commands
findings.evidence: run_command() passes the model-supplied `command` string to subprocess.run(command, shell=True) with no allowlist, no argument parsing and no sandbox. It is registered in REGISTRY (line 141) and advertised to the model in TOOL_SCHEMAS as a free-form string with description 'Run a read-only diagnostic shell command' — a description the model is under no obligation to honour and which the code does not enforce.
findings.impact: Whatever steers the model steers a shell on the support box: full remote code execution with the service's privileges and its credentials, including DESKAGENT_GATEWAY_KEY and DESKAGENT_SERVICE_TOKEN in the process environment. Reachable through the chat endpoint and, without any authentication at all, through the ticket-injection path in planner.py:73.
findings.recommendation: Delete the free-form shell tool. If live diagnostics are required, expose a fixed set of parameterised commands invoked with a list argv and shell=False, validate every argument against a strict pattern, and run them under a restricted account.

findings.title: SQL injection in the shipments route via order id and carrier
findings.evidence: The shipments handler concatenates req.params.id (line 77) and req.query.carrier (line 78) directly into a quoted SQL string and calls query(sql) with no parameter array, so mysql2 receives a fully-formed statement. Every other query in this file uses ? placeholders, so the escape is a local regression, not a project convention.
findings.impact: Any signed-in merchant user reads or modifies arbitrary rows across the whole database (orders and users of every other merchant), and can pivot to file or command primitives that the database grants.
findings.recommendation: Use ? placeholders for both values and drop the conditional string concatenation, matching the other handlers in this file.

findings.title: Zip Slip: archive member paths are joined without validation
findings.evidence: extract_zip() computes `target = dest / info.filename` and writes straight to it. The only filter is _interesting(), which drops .DS_Store/__MACOSX/Thumbs.db by name. There is no containment check at all: a member named ../../../../etc/cron.d/x escapes dest, and because pathlib's / operator lets an absolute operand replace the base, a member named /home/user/.ssh/authorized_keys writes to that exact path. The tar path in the same module implements the containment check properly in _safe_tar_members (lines 71-73) and the test suite covers it only for tar (tests/test_extract.py:42), so zip bundles are entirely unguarded.
findings.impact: Installing an untrusted .zip bundle writes attacker-chosen files anywhere the process can reach — cron entries, shell rc files, authorized_keys, or a library on sys.path — which is code execution as the installing user.
findings.recommendation: Apply the same resolved-containment check used by _safe_tar_members to every zip member before opening the output file, and reject absolute names and .. segments outright.

findings.title: Bundle manifest parsed with the unsafe YAML loader
findings.evidence: load_manifest() reads packmate.yaml — a file that ships inside the untrusted bundle — with yaml.load(fh, Loader=yaml.Loader). yaml.Loader is PyYAML's unsafe loader and constructs arbitrary Python objects from tags such as !!python/object/apply:os.system. The docstring justifies it by wanting tuples and datetimes in metadata. load_lockfile() twelve lines below uses yaml.safe_load() on a file from the same archive, so the safe primitive was known and deliberately not used here.
findings.impact: Merely running `packmate install` on a hostile bundle executes attacker code as the installing user, before any signature or digest check. No user interaction beyond installing the bundle.
findings.recommendation: Use yaml.safe_load(); if timestamps really are needed, keep them as ISO strings and parse them explicitly after loading.

findings.title: Chain: outside pull request escalates to full AWS account takeover
findings.evidence: Step 1: deploy.yml triggers on pull_request_target (line 6), which runs with the base repository's secrets, and checks out the proposer's commit (line 27). Step 2: terraform init/plan (lines 43, 50) executes the attacker's configuration on the runner while TF_VAR_db_master_password is set. Step 3: the job has already assumed secrets.DEPLOYER_ROLE_ARN (line 38); that role's inline policy is Action '*' on Resource '*' (iam.tf:80), and its OIDC trust policy has no aud condition and a wildcard sub (iam.tf:58). Step 4: permissions write-all (line 9) hands the same run a fully-privileged GITHUB_TOKEN. The uploaded tfplan artifact (line 53) leaks the database password even without step 2.
findings.impact: An unprivileged outside contributor obtains AWS account administrator and repository write in a single pull request, with no human approval in the path. Independently, the same estate exposes RDS to 0.0.0.0/0 with a committed master password, so the account and the data have two disjoint compromise paths.
findings.recommendation: Split validation of untrusted code onto pull_request with no secrets; scope the deployer policy and add StringEquals on :aud plus a specific :sub; set least-privilege job permissions; stop uploading raw plan files.

findings.title: Deploy workflow runs untrusted PR code under pull_request_target with AWS credentials
findings.evidence: The workflow triggers on pull_request_target (line 6), which runs in the base repository's context with access to secrets, and the plan job then checks out ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }} (line 27) — the proposer's code. It assumes secrets.DEPLOYER_ROLE_ARN (line 38) and runs `terraform init` and `terraform plan` (lines 43, 50) over that checked-out tree with TF_VAR_db_master_password in the environment. Terraform executes attacker-controlled configuration: a malicious provider block, an external data source or a local-exec provisioner runs during plan, before any human approves.
findings.impact: Any outside contributor who opens a pull request executes code on the runner with the deployer role — which carries Action:*/Resource:* per iam.tf:80 — and with the RDS master password in the environment. Full AWS account compromise from an unprivileged PR.
findings.recommendation: Use pull_request for validation of untrusted code and never check out PR head under pull_request_target. If the two must be combined, gate on an explicit environment approval, drop credentials from the plan job, and run terraform plan with -lock=false against a read-only role.

findings.title: CI deployer role grants Action * on Resource *
findings.evidence: The deployer role's inline policy is a single statement with Action = "*" and Resource = "*" — unconditional account administrator. The comment explains it as covering 'occasionally a stray resource nobody scoped yet'. The sibling task role directly above shows the intended pattern: scoped resources plus an aws:SourceVpce condition.
findings.impact: Any compromise of the GitHub Actions workflow that assumes this role is a full AWS account takeover: read every bucket, alter IAM, delete backups, create persistence. It also removes any blast-radius limit on the pull_request_target flaw in deploy.yml.
findings.recommendation: Replace with least-privilege statements for the ECS, ECR, S3 and SSM actions the pipeline actually performs, scoped to this stack's resource ARNs.

findings.title: Production Postgres is internet-reachable on 5432
findings.evidence: The db security group allows tcp/5432 ingress from cidr_blocks ["0.0.0.0/0"] (line 20), and aws_db_instance.main sets publicly_accessible = true (line 49), so the instance gets a public endpoint that resolves globally. The comment explains it as a stopgap while a VPN peering request is queued. The instance is placed in private subnets, but publicly_accessible overrides that intent, and the read replica shares the same wide-open security group (line 70) despite setting publicly_accessible = false itself.
findings.impact: Every host on the internet can reach the billing database directly and attempt authentication. Paired with the master password committed at rds.tf:45 this is a direct, unauthenticated path to all customer and invoice data with no application layer in between.
findings.recommendation: Set publicly_accessible = false, restrict ingress to the app security group id (as main.tf does for the app tier), and route analyst access through a bastion or VPN rather than a public listener.

findings.title: JWT signature verification disabled in decode_token
findings.evidence: decode_token() calls jwt.decode(token, options={"verify_signature": False}) with no key and no algorithms list. current_user() feeds those unverified claims straight into User(id=..., org_id=..., role=...). The docstring justifies this by asserting the edge gateway already checked the signature, but the service binds 0.0.0.0:8000 in its own container (Dockerfile CMD) and no gateway exists in this repository, so the assumption is unverifiable and not enforced in code.
findings.impact: Any unauthenticated caller can mint a token with an arbitrary sub/org/role and become any user in any tenant, including role=admin, which unlocks every /api/admin route. Complete authentication and authorization bypass.
findings.recommendation: Verify with jwt.decode(token, settings.secret_key, algorithms=["HS256"]) and let PyJWT enforce exp/iat; never accept unsigned claims.

findings.title: Chain: unauthenticated remote code execution in the billing API
findings.evidence: Two individually-valid findings compose into an unauthenticated RCE. Step 1: decode_token (auth.py:51) accepts an unsigned token, so an anonymous caller mints claims with role=admin (reproduced, workspace/repro poc4). Step 2: require_admin (auth.py:83) is satisfied by that forged role. Step 3: export_ledger (routes_admin.py:53) interpolates the period path segment into a shell string executed with shell=True. The 'mounted behind the ops VPN' comment at routes_admin.py:1 is the only stated barrier and is not enforced anywhere in code; the Dockerfile binds 0.0.0.0:8000.
findings.impact: Anonymous shell on the billing service, with settings.secret_key and the Postgres DSN in process memory. Neither step requires credentials, a stolen token, or user interaction.
findings.recommendation: Fix either link to break the chain, but fix both: verify the JWT signature with the secret key, and invoke the exporter with a list argv after validating period against ^\d{4}-\d{2}$.

findings.title: OS command injection in ledger export period parameter
findings.evidence: export_ledger() interpolates the URL path segment `period` into a shell string (lines 53-56) and runs it with subprocess.run(cmd, shell=True). The docstring assumes period is a YYYY-MM string from a date picker, but FastAPI declares it as a bare `str` path parameter with no pattern constraint, so any shell metacharacter reaches /bin/sh. The sibling route rebuild_search_index() shows the correct list-argv form.
findings.impact: Remote code execution as the pulse user inside the API container. Chained with the JWT bypass in auth.py:51 (which lets anyone claim role=admin) this is unauthenticated RCE.
findings.recommendation: Validate period against ^\d{4}-\d{2}$ and invoke the exporter with a list argv and shell=False, as rebuild_search_index already does.

findings.title: SQL injection in invoice search via q and sort parameters
findings.evidence: search_invoices() builds the statement with f-strings: `number ILIKE '%{q}%'` (line 51) and `ORDER BY {sort} {direction}` (line 52), then executes it with text(sql) and no bind parameters. q and sort come straight off the query string. Only `direction` is validated against SORT_DIRECTIONS; `sort` has no allowlist even though db.py demonstrates the correct ROLLUP_COLUMNS pattern for exactly this problem.
findings.impact: Authenticated tenant breaks out of the string literal to read or modify any row in the database, including other tenants' invoices and the users table with its password hashes; ORDER BY injection additionally supports blind boolean/subquery exfiltration.
findings.recommendation: Bind q as a parameter (:q with a LIKE pattern) and resolve sort through an allowlist dict mapping API names to real column names, like db.ROLLUP_COLUMNS already does.

findings.title: Untrusted ticket text is concatenated into the system prompt
findings.evidence: gather_context() takes ticket bodies matched by a substring search over the user's question and formats them as 'Operator notes from related tickets:' lines. build_system_prompt() then appends that block to the SYSTEM prompt (prompts.py:53-57) — the highest-trust channel, described in the code comment as 'where the model looks for background it should treat as settled'. Ticket bodies are written by whoever files a ticket, and nothing sanitises, delimits or marks them as untrusted data.
findings.impact: Anyone who can file a support ticket plants instructions that the model reads with system-level authority on some later, unrelated conversation. Combined with run_command in tools.py:68 this is unauthenticated remote code execution: the attacker never authenticates to deskagent at all.
findings.recommendation: Never place retrieved content in the system prompt. Pass it as a user-role message inside explicit delimiters, state in the system prompt that retrieved ticket text is untrusted data and never an instruction, and require human approval for any state-changing tool call.

findings.title: LLM tool reads any file the process can open
findings.evidence: read_file() takes the model-supplied path, expands ~, and returns up to 200 KB of it. There is no base directory, no containment check and no extension filter — the docstring states the path is 'taken as given' because runbooks live in several places. The result is returned to the caller in the response steps array (planner.py:115).
findings.impact: The model can be induced to read /etc/passwd, /proc/self/environ (which yields the gateway key and the service token), ~/.ssh/id_rsa, or any application secret on the box, and the content is echoed back to whoever is talking to the assistant.
findings.recommendation: Resolve the path against a fixed allowlist of runbook directories, verify the resolved path stays inside one of them, and refuse symlinks that leave the root.

findings.title: SSRF: upstream allowlist is a substring match on the whole URL
findings.evidence: fetchRemote() admits a target if strings.Contains(target, "assets.example.net") or either of two sibling hosts matches anywhere in the URL string (lines 64-66). It never parses the URL, so the check is satisfied by the path, the query, the userinfo or a suffixed domain: http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/?x=assets.example.net, http://assets.example.net.attacker.tld/, or http://attacker.tld/#assets.example.net all pass. The scheme is not constrained either. /thumb reaches this with no authentication (main.go:95).
findings.impact: Unauthenticated attackers make the proxy issue arbitrary GET requests from inside the VPC — cloud instance metadata (IAM credentials), internal admin panels, and services on 127.0.0.1 — and receive the decoded result back as an image or an error oracle.
findings.recommendation: Parse with url.Parse, require scheme https, compare u.Hostname() for exact equality against the knownOrigins values, and resolve plus re-check the address to block redirects and DNS rebinding to link-local and private ranges.

findings.title: Session cookie is not httpOnly and not secure
findings.evidence: The session cookie config sets httpOnly:false and secure:false with a 24-hour maxAge. server.js passes this object straight into express-session, so the odsid cookie is readable by page JavaScript and is transmitted over plaintext HTTP.
findings.impact: Turns the stored XSS in lib/render.js:61 from a defacement into a full session takeover, and exposes the session to any network observer when TLS is not terminated in front. Neither flag has a legitimate reason to be off for a session identifier.
findings.recommendation: Set httpOnly:true and secure:true (with trust proxy already configured at server.js:21), and consider sameSite:'strict'.

findings.title: Hardcoded express-session secret in committed configuration
findings.evidence: session.secret is the literal 'orderdesk-session-4b1f9c02ae77' in config/default.json, which server.js reads via config.get('session.secret'). The mysql password in the same file is correctly sourced from process.env.MYSQL_PASSWORD (lib/db.js:17), so the session key is an inconsistent exception.
findings.impact: Anyone with repository or image access forges signed session cookies for any userId/merchantId and authenticates as any merchant without credentials.
findings.recommendation: Load the secret from the environment with no committed default, fail to boot when it is missing, and rotate the leaked value.

findings.title: Stored XSS: customer_note is interpolated into HTML unescaped
findings.evidence: renderOrder() escapes order.reference, order.customer_name, order.status and every line field with escapeHtml(), but writes `${order.customer_note || ''}` raw into the note div. The comment states this is deliberate so packers see the note 'exactly as written'. customer_note is free text a shopper types at checkout, and the page is served with res.type('html') from routes/orders.js:63.
findings.impact: A shopper stores script in a checkout note that executes in the fulfilment console when staff open the order. The session cookie is readable from JavaScript (httpOnly is false in config/default.json:15), so the payload steals the staff session and acts as that merchant user.
findings.recommendation: Escape customer_note with the existing escapeHtml() helper; if formatting is genuinely required, render it as pre-wrapped text or run it through a sanitiser allowlist.

findings.title: Chain: shopper-supplied checkout note takes over a merchant session and then the database
findings.evidence: Step 1: a shopper stores script in customer_note, which renderOrder writes into the page unescaped (render.js:61) while escaping every neighbouring field. Step 2: warehouse staff open the order detail page (routes/orders.js:63) and the payload runs. Step 3: the session cookie is configured httpOnly:false (config/default.json:15), so the payload reads document.cookie directly rather than needing a same-origin request. Step 4: with that session the attacker reaches GET /api/orders/:id/shipments, whose SQL is built by string concatenation (routes/orders.js:77), and reads the whole database including other merchants' rows.
findings.impact: A party who only placed an order escalates to arbitrary SQL against the fulfilment database. Each link is independently valid; together they turn a checkout text field into full data compromise.
findings.recommendation: Escape customer_note with the existing escapeHtml helper, set httpOnly and secure on the session cookie, and parameterise the shipments query.

findings.title: Start script disables Node TLS certificate validation process-wide
findings.evidence: The production start script is `NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=0 node server.js`. This is not scoped to one client or one host: it disables certificate and hostname verification for every TLS connection the process makes, including the mysql2 pool and any outbound HTTP.
findings.impact: Any attacker who can intercept traffic from the app container — to the database, the payments provider, or an internal service — can present any certificate and read or rewrite the connection silently.
findings.recommendation: Remove the variable from the start script; supply the internal CA to the specific client that needs it via the ca option or NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS.

findings.title: postinstall hook pipes a remote script into a shell
findings.evidence: The postinstall lifecycle script is `curl -fsSL https://tooling.orderdesk.internal/hooks/bootstrap.sh | sh`. It runs automatically on every npm install — developer laptops, CI runners and image builds — fetching unpinned, unverified code over the network and executing it immediately.
findings.impact: Whoever controls that host, its DNS, or its TLS path (trivial here because the start script also disables TLS verification) achieves code execution on every machine that installs the project, including the CI runner that holds deployment credentials.
findings.recommendation: Remove the lifecycle hook; vendor the bootstrap step as a reviewed, checksum-verified file invoked explicitly, never piped from the network into a shell.

findings.title: Missing merchant scoping on order detail endpoint (IDOR)
findings.evidence: The order detail route runs `SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = ?` with only req.params.id and never compares order.merchant_id to req.session.merchantId. The list route above it filters on merchant_id and the cancel route below it (line 91) includes `AND merchant_id = ?`, so this handler is the only one in the file that omits the tenant predicate.
findings.impact: Any authenticated merchant user reads any other merchant's order by id, including the full row from SELECT * and the order lines. Cross-tenant data breach.
findings.recommendation: Add `AND merchant_id = ?` with req.session.merchantId, and select explicit columns rather than *.

findings.title: Install destination is derived from attacker-controlled manifest fields
findings.evidence: cmd_install() builds `target = dest / manifest.slug`, where slug is f"{name}-{version}" straight from the bundle's own manifest (manifest.py:34) with no character validation. It then calls shutil.rmtree(target) if it exists (line 53) and shutil.move(workdir, target) (line 54). A manifest declaring name: ../../../../home/user/.config escapes the destination directory in both operations.
findings.impact: A hostile bundle deletes an arbitrary directory tree the user can write and then plants its own contents at that path — destructive and a persistence primitive, independent of the zip and YAML issues above.
findings.recommendation: Validate name and version against ^[A-Za-z0-9._-]+$ before building slug, and verify the resolved target is inside the resolved dest before any rmtree or move.

findings.title: Deploy workflow grants the GITHUB_TOKEN write-all permissions
findings.evidence: The deploy workflow sets `permissions: write-all` at the top level, giving the automatic GITHUB_TOKEN write access to every scope — contents, packages, actions, id-token, deployments. ci.yml in the same directory sets `permissions: contents: read`, so the restrictive baseline is understood in this repository.
findings.impact: Any code execution inside this workflow — trivially reachable via the pull_request_target checkout on line 27 — can push commits, publish packages, rewrite workflow files and mint id-tokens, converting a single run into persistent control of the repository.
findings.recommendation: Declare the minimum scopes the jobs need (contents: read, id-token: write for OIDC) at the job level instead of write-all.

findings.title: GitHub OIDC trust policy lacks an audience condition and accepts any repository ref
findings.evidence: The assume-role policy for the deployer conditions only on token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub with StringLike "repo:example-net/orderdesk:*". There is no condition on token.actions.githubusercontent.com:aud, which AWS documents as required — without it any GitHub-issued token presented to the STS endpoint satisfies the audience. The sub wildcard additionally matches every branch, tag, pull request and environment of the repository rather than a specific ref or environment.
findings.impact: The missing aud condition weakens the boundary that is supposed to make OIDC federation safe, and the wildcard sub means a workflow on any branch — including one added by the pull_request_target path — assumes a role that holds Action:*/Resource:*.
findings.recommendation: Add a StringEquals condition on :aud equal to sts.amazonaws.com, and narrow :sub to the specific ref or environment permitted to deploy, e.g. repo:example-net/orderdesk:environment:production.

findings.title: RDS master password hardcoded in Terraform
findings.evidence: aws_db_instance.main sets password = "Pg-orderdesk-2024-rotate-me" as a literal. variables.tf:39 declares a sensitive db_master_password with a 24-character validation rule and a comment stating there is deliberately no default so plan fails loudly — but rds.tf never references it, and both workflow jobs still export TF_VAR_db_master_password. The safe mechanism exists, is wired through CI, and is simply not used.
findings.impact: The production database master credential is in the repository, in every clone and CI log context, and in the Terraform state in the orderdesk-tfstate bucket. Combined with the public 5432 listener above it is directly usable by anyone who reads the repo.
findings.recommendation: Replace the literal with var.db_master_password (or manage_master_user_password with Secrets Manager), rotate the exposed credential, and treat the state bucket as compromised for this value.

findings.title: Artifacts S3 bucket is world-readable
findings.evidence: The artifacts bucket sets acl = "public-read" (line 34) and its public access block turns off all four guards — block_public_acls, block_public_policy, ignore_public_acls and restrict_public_buckets are all false (lines 13-16), with an explicit depends_on so the ACL is applied after the guards are removed. The comment says signed URLs never landed. The logs bucket in the same file (lines 69-76) sets all four to true, so the intended baseline is clear.
findings.impact: Anonymous internet users list and download every object in the build-artifact bucket — application bundles, and anything else the pipeline writes there, which commonly includes configuration and credentials.
findings.recommendation: Set all four public access block flags to true, drop the public-read ACL, and serve the CDN through an origin access identity or presigned URLs.

findings.title: Missing tenant scoping on invoice detail endpoint (IDOR)
findings.evidence: get_invoice() selects `FROM invoices WHERE id = :id` with no org_id predicate and never compares row['org_id'] to user.org_id, even though it selects the column. The invoice line items are then fetched by the same unchecked id. db.org_of_invoice() exists for exactly this check and is never called; delete_invoice() at line 132 does scope by org_id, so the omission is inconsistent within the same file.
findings.impact: Any authenticated tenant enumerates sequential integer ids to read every invoice in the system: amounts, notes, customer line items. Cross-tenant data breach.
findings.recommendation: Add `AND org_id = :org_id` to the query (or call org_of_invoice and 404 on mismatch) exactly as delete_invoice does.

findings.title: Hardcoded JWT signing key in source
findings.evidence: Settings.secret_key defaults to the literal 'pulse-hs256-2f8ab91c4d7e0356' and there is no os.environ override for it, unlike database_url, environment, ledger_base_url and export_dir which all go through _env(). The value is committed and is the HS256 key used by issue_token() at auth.py:41.
findings.impact: Anyone with read access to the repository, the image, or a leaked file can forge valid session tokens for any user and role. Rotation requires a code change and a redeploy of every process that mints tokens.
findings.recommendation: Read the key from the environment or a secret store with no in-code default, fail closed at startup when it is absent, and rotate the committed value.

findings.title: No per-caller authorization on session identifiers
findings.evidence: Authentication is a single shared service token checked in the before_request hook (server.py:41-45), presented by the helpdesk UI and the Slack relay on behalf of every end user. /v1/chat then accepts any session_id from the request body and loads its history, and DELETE /v1/sessions/<id> deletes any session, with no notion of who owns it. The only protection is that ids are uuid4.
findings.impact: Any caller holding the shared token — or any end user of a relay that forwards a caller-supplied session_id — reads or destroys another user's conversation history, which may contain the file contents and command output produced by the tools above.
findings.recommendation: Bind each session to an authenticated end-user identity at creation and verify that identity on every load, save and delete, rather than relying on identifier unguessability.

findings.title: Model-supplied tool arguments are splatted into the callable unvalidated
findings.evidence: dispatch() looks up the callable and calls fn(**arguments) with the raw `input` object from the model reply (planner.py:105). The declared input_schema in TOOL_SCHEMAS is sent to the model but is never enforced on the way back — no type check, no required-key check, no bound on numeric fields. planner.py catches the resulting TypeError with a broad `except Exception` and keeps the loop running.
findings.impact: The model (or an injected instruction) sets run_command's timeout to an arbitrary integer, holding a worker for as long as it likes, or probes callables with unexpected keyword shapes. It removes the last place where a malformed or hostile tool call could have been rejected before execution.
findings.recommendation: Validate `arguments` against the tool's declared input_schema (jsonschema) before dispatch, reject unknown keys, and clamp numeric parameters to server-side bounds.

findings.title: http_get allowlist is bypassed by an upstream redirect
findings.evidence: http_get() checks parts.hostname against ALLOWED_HOSTS and the scheme against https, then calls urlopen(). urllib follows 3xx redirects automatically and the allowlist is applied only to the original URL, never re-checked on the redirect target — which may be http, an internal host, or 169.254.169.254.
findings.impact: One of the three documentation hosts (or anything able to answer for them) redirects the assistant to an arbitrary internal endpoint and the body comes back to the model and, via the steps transcript, to the caller. The exact-hostname check the comment relies on holds only for the first hop.
findings.recommendation: Install an opener with redirects disabled and re-run the allowlist check on every hop, or fetch with a client that exposes and validates the final URL before returning the body.

findings.title: Predictable world-readable staging file created without O_EXCL
findings.evidence: stagePath() builds a fully predictable name in the shared temp directory — os.TempDir() + "edgeproxy-stage-" + key + ".part" — where key is a SHA-1 of attacker-supplied inputs and is therefore computable in advance. writeStaged() opens it with O_WRONLY|O_CREATE|O_TRUNC and mode 0644: no O_EXCL, no private directory, world-readable.
findings.impact: Any local user pre-creates that path as a symlink and the proxy truncates and overwrites the target file with its own privileges; failing that, the 0644 mode leaks cached object content to every account on the host. The cache directory itself is created 0750 (cache.go:47), so the staging path is the weak half.
findings.recommendation: Create the scratch file with os.CreateTemp in a directory owned by the service with 0700, or open with O_EXCL and mode 0600 and treat an existing path as an error.

findings.title: TLS certificate verification disabled on the upstream HTTP client
findings.evidence: upstreamClient is constructed with tls.Config{InsecureSkipVerify: true}. MinVersion is set to TLS 1.2, which makes the setting look considered, but InsecureSkipVerify disables both chain and hostname validation for every request the proxy makes.
findings.impact: An attacker on the path to the origin fleet serves any certificate and substitutes the image bytes the proxy caches and redistributes, or harvests any credential the proxy would send. Combined with the substring allowlist above, the attacker also chooses the destination.
findings.recommendation: Remove InsecureSkipVerify and load the internal CA into the transport's RootCAs pool.

findings.title: Wildcard version range on the node-fetch dependency
findings.evidence: node-fetch is declared as "*" while every other dependency uses a caret range. A wildcard resolves to whatever the registry currently publishes as latest, including a new major version or a compromised release.
findings.impact: Any install can silently pull a different, unreviewed version of a package that performs outbound HTTP, giving an attacker who compromises the package a direct path into the fulfilment service.
findings.recommendation: Pin node-fetch to an explicit range and commit a lockfile so installs are reproducible.

findings.title: Session is not regenerated on successful login (session fixation)
findings.evidence: The login handler assigns req.session.userId and req.session.merchantId onto the session that already existed for the request. req.session.regenerate() is never called, so the pre-authentication session identifier survives the privilege transition. The logout path does call destroy(), showing the API was available.
findings.impact: An attacker who can plant a known odsid value in a victim's browser — straightforward given secure:false and httpOnly:false in config/default.json — holds a session that becomes fully authenticated the moment the victim logs in.
findings.recommendation: Call req.session.regenerate() before writing the identity fields, and re-save the session afterwards.

findings.title: Bundle digest verification is optional and off by default
findings.evidence: download() only compares digests when expected_sha256 is truthy: `if expected_sha256 and got != expected_sha256.lower()`. cmd_pull passes `args.sha256 or ""` and the --sha256 argument defaults to an empty string (cli.py:104), so the ordinary `packmate pull name version` path downloads and returns a bundle with no integrity verification whatsoever — the digest is computed and logged but never checked.
findings.impact: Anything that can serve or tamper with the registry response supplies a substituted bundle, which then flows into the unsafe extract and manifest paths. The security control is present in the code but inert on the default path.
findings.recommendation: Require a pinned digest (from the lockfile) for every download, or fail closed when none is supplied; treat an absent expectation as an error, not as a skip.

findings.title: Deploy workflow pins actions to mutable refs
findings.evidence: deploy.yml uses hashicorp/setup-terraform@master (line 31) — a branch that moves with every upstream commit — plus actions/checkout@v4 (lines 25, 66), aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4 (lines 36, 69) and actions/upload-artifact@v4 (line 53), all mutable tags. ci.yml in the same directory pins every action to a full commit SHA with the version in a trailing comment and verifies its tflint download against a sha256, so the hardened pattern exists and was simply not applied to the workflow that holds credentials.
findings.impact: A compromised upstream action, or a tag repointed by an attacker who gains that repository, executes in the job that assumes the AWS deployer role and holds the database password.
findings.recommendation: Pin every action to a full commit SHA with the version as a comment, exactly as ci.yml does, and enable Dependabot for action updates.

findings.title: Terraform plan artifact is uploaded and retained
findings.evidence: The plan job writes terraform/tfplan (line 50) and uploads it as a build artifact with five-day retention (lines 52-57). The plan is produced with TF_VAR_db_master_password set, and a binary plan file records resource attribute values including credentials; Terraform marks them sensitive for console output only, not inside the plan file.
findings.impact: Anyone with read access to the repository — including, under pull_request_target, the author of an outside pull request — downloads the artifact and extracts the RDS master password and the full infrastructure layout via `terraform show -json tfplan`.
findings.recommendation: Do not upload raw plan files. Publish a redacted human-readable summary instead, or keep the plan in the job and gate apply behind an environment approval.

findings.title: Outbound TLS certificate verification disabled for the ledger service
findings.evidence: verify_ssl defaults to False and is passed as `verify=settings.verify_ssl` to requests.post() in sync_ledger (routes_admin.py:93). The comment explains this was done because a sandbox CA broke CI, but the flag is global and applies in production, where ledger_base_url points at https://ledger.internal.pulsebilling.io.
findings.impact: An attacker positioned on the path to the ledger service can intercept and modify billing synchronisation traffic, including the admin email in the request body and the ledger's JSON response, with no certificate warning.
findings.recommendation: Set verify to the internal CA bundle path (requests accepts a CA file for `verify`) instead of False, and keep verification on in every environment.

findings.title: Debug mode on by default exposes stack traces to API clients
findings.evidence: Settings.debug defaults to True with no environment override, while `environment` defaults to 'production'. The global exception handler in main.py (lines 100-102) branches on settings.debug to add `detail` (the exception string) and `trace` (traceback.format_exc()) to every 500 response body, and main.py:21 also drops the log level to DEBUG.
findings.impact: Unhandled errors return full Python tracebacks to any caller: file paths, module layout, SQL fragments and frequently the values that triggered the error. This materially assists exploitation of the SQL and command injection flaws in the same service.
findings.recommendation: Default debug to False, drive it from an environment variable, and never include exception text or tracebacks in a response body.

findings.title: Tool output is returned to the caller in the response transcript
findings.evidence: run_turn() appends {"tool": name, "input": args, "output": output[:2000]} to the transcript for every tool call, and server.py returns that list to the client as `steps`. The system prompt asks the model never to repeat credentials it encounters, but the transcript bypasses the model entirely — raw tool output is serialised to the response whatever it contains.
findings.impact: Anything read_file or run_command produced — file contents, environment variables, command stderr — reaches the caller verbatim even when the model's own answer would have withheld it. The prompt-level control at prompts.py:15 does not apply to this path.
findings.recommendation: Return only tool names and status in the transcript, or redact the output server-side against a secret pattern list before serialising it.

findings.title: Admin token comparison leaks token length before the constant-time check
findings.evidence: checkToken() returns false immediately when len(got) != len(want), before reaching subtle.ConstantTimeCompare. The length test itself is the oracle: the caller learns the exact secret length from response timing and from which requests reach the comparison at all.
findings.impact: Reduces the search space for the operator token guarding /admin/stats and /admin/purge. Minor on its own, and the comparison of equal-length candidates is correctly constant time.
findings.recommendation: Hash both sides to a fixed width (for example SHA-256) and compare the digests with subtle.ConstantTimeCompare, so no branch depends on the secret's length.

findings.title: SHA-1 used to derive cache keys
findings.evidence: cacheKey() derives the on-disk object name with sha1.Sum over the concatenated target, width and format. SHA-1 is collision-prone, and the key is also used to build the predictable staging filename in stagePath().
findings.impact: An attacker able to craft colliding inputs can make two distinct upstream objects share one cache entry, poisoning what other clients receive. The practical bar is high for this input shape, but the primitive should not be SHA-1 in new code.
findings.recommendation: Switch to SHA-256 (crypto/sha256) for the cache key; the field is opaque so the change is a one-line swap plus a cache flush.

findings.title: Migration filename is interpolated into a mysql -e statement
findings.evidence: applyMigration() constrains the path with path.basename() and uses execFile, so no shell is involved — but the basename is then embedded in the SQL text `source ${file}` passed to mysql's -e flag. A filename containing a semicolon or quote is interpreted by the mysql client as additional statements, not as part of a path.
findings.impact: Anyone who can place or rename a file in the migrations directory executes arbitrary SQL as the orderdesk database user the next time migrations run. Reachable only with write access to the deployment tree, so exposure is limited.
findings.recommendation: Validate the filename against ^[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+\.sql$ before use, or feed the file to the client on stdin instead of composing an -e statement.

findings.title: Password digest compared with a non-constant-time operator
findings.evidence: The login handler compares the derived PBKDF2 digest with `digest !== user.password_hash`, a short-circuiting string comparison, rather than crypto.timingSafeEqual. The same file imports node:crypto already, and the webhook path in routes/webhooks.js:48 uses timingSafeEqual correctly, so the primitive was available.
findings.impact: Leaks a per-byte timing signal on the stored hash comparison. Additionally, no dummy hash is computed when the user row is missing, so response latency distinguishes existing accounts from non-existent ones and enables user enumeration.
findings.recommendation: Compare with crypto.timingSafeEqual over equal-length buffers, and compute a dummy PBKDF2 digest when no user row is found so both paths cost the same.

findings.title: Security groups allow unrestricted egress to the internet
findings.evidence: The app security group (line 107), the ALB group (line 85) and the database group (rds.tf:27) each allow all protocols and ports to 0.0.0.0/0 on egress. Ingress is scoped carefully for the app tier — from the ALB security group only — so the asymmetry is deliberate convenience rather than an oversight in the ingress model.
findings.impact: Removes any network-layer brake on exfiltration or command-and-control from a compromised task; with the SSRF in edgeproxy and the shell tool in deskagent both reachable in this estate, egress filtering is the control that would contain them.
findings.recommendation: Restrict egress to the specific destinations each tier needs — VPC endpoints, the database port, and the package mirror — rather than allowing everything.

findings.title: Container image installs dependencies without hash pinning
findings.evidence: The image runs `pip install --require-hashes=false -r requirements.txt`. requirements.txt pins versions but carries no hashes, and the flag explicitly turns the hash check off rather than leaving it at its default.
findings.impact: A compromised index or a mirror that serves a substituted artifact for a pinned version is installed without detection, executing attacker code at build time and in production.
findings.recommendation: Generate a hashed requirements file (pip-compile --generate-hashes) and install with --require-hashes.

findings.title: Login throttle is per-process and its keyspace is unbounded
findings.evidence: _login_attempts is a module-level dict in one process. The Dockerfile CMD starts uvicorn with --workers 4, so the effective limit is 4x the intended 5 attempts per minute and resets on every restart. Entries are inserted per distinct client_ip and never evicted or bounded — expired windows are reset in place but the key stays forever.
findings.impact: Credential stuffing gets four times the intended budget, and an attacker spraying spoofed or rotated source addresses grows the dict without limit until the worker exhausts memory.
findings.recommendation: Move the counter to shared storage (Redis) keyed by IP and account, and bound or expire the keyspace.

findings.title: Login attempts log the submitted email address at INFO
findings.evidence: login() logs an f-string containing body.email, the client IP and the raw User-Agent header on every attempt, before authentication succeeds or fails, with no redaction configured.
findings.impact: Account identifiers and client metadata accumulate in log aggregation for both successful and failed attempts, widening the blast radius of log access and creating a record of which addresses have accounts.
findings.recommendation: Log a hash or an internal user id instead of the raw address, and keep unauthenticated request metadata out of INFO.
